title: Input and Output
summary: `std::cout <<` sends values **out** to the screen. `std::cin >>` brings values **in** from the keyboard. The arrows point the way the data moves.
markdown:
## Follow the arrows A program that cannot show anything or ask anything is not much use. C++ gives you two tools for talking to the person at the keyboard. ```mermaid flowchart LR V1["a value"] -->|"<<"| COUT["std::cout
(the screen)"] KB["std::cin
(the keyboard)"] -->|">>"| V2["a variable"] ``` | You write | Read it as | Data moves | |---|---|---| | `std::cout << x;` | "send x to the screen" | from `x` **to** the screen | | `std::cin >> x;` | "read from the keyboard into x" | from the keyboard **to** `x` | If you ever forget which arrows go with which, look at where they point. ## Printing with `std::cout` ```cpp #include int main() { int apples{ 5 }; std::cout << "I have " << apples << " apples\n"; std::cout << "Line 1\n" << "Line 2\n"; return 0; } ``` ``` I have 5 apples Line 1 Line 2 ``` Three things to notice: - You can chain several `<<` in one statement. Each piece is printed in order. - Text in quotes is printed exactly as written. A variable name **without** quotes prints the value inside the variable. - `std::cout` adds nothing for you. No spaces, no new lines. If you want a space between two things, put it inside the quotes. ### Special characters A backslash inside quotes starts a code for a character you cannot simply type. | Code | What it prints | |---|---| | `\n` | the start of a new line | | `\t` | a tab (a jump to the next column) | | `\"` | a double quote | | `\\` | one backslash | > [!note] You will also see `std::endl` > `std::cout << "Hi" << std::endl;` also ends the line. It does a little extra work each time, so this course uses `\n`, which is the normal choice. ## Reading with `std::cin` ```cpp #include int main() { std::cout << "Enter your age: "; int age{}; std::cin >> age; std::cout << "In 10 years you will be " << age + 10 << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ``` Enter your age: 21 In 10 years you will be 31 ``` The steps are always the same: ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Print a question"] --> B["Create a variable
to hold the answer"] --> C["std::cin >> variable"] --> D["Use the variable"] ``` The program stops at `std::cin >>` and waits until the person types something and presses Enter. ### Reading two values ```cpp int width{}; int height{}; std::cin >> width >> height; ``` The person can type `3 7` on one line, or `3`, Enter, `7`, Enter. `std::cin >>` skips spaces and new lines to find the next value. ### Reading a whole line of text `std::cin >>` stops at the first space. That is fine for a number, but wrong for a full name. ```cpp #include #include int main() { std::cout << "Your full name: "; std::string name{}; std::getline(std::cin >> std::ws, name); std::cout << "Hello, " << name << "!\n"; return 0; } ``` | Typed | `std::cin >> name` stores | `std::getline(std::cin >> std::ws, name)` stores | |---|---|---| | `Ada Lovelace` | `Ada` | `Ada Lovelace` | For now, treat `std::getline(std::cin >> std::ws, name)` as the recipe for "read the rest of the line". The `std::ws` part skips any leftover Enter from an earlier answer. ## Two mistakes to expect | Mistake | What happens | |---|---| | Arrows the wrong way: `std::cin << x` | A long, confusing compile error. Check the arrows first. | | Typing letters when the program wants a number | The read fails and the variable is left at 0. You will learn to handle this in [[3.07 Input Validation and assert]]. | ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Which way do the arrows point for input? - `std::cin << variable;`, towards the keyboard + `std::cin >> variable;`, from the keyboard into the variable - `variable >> std::cin;`, from the variable to the keyboard - Either way; the direction does not matter > For input the data moves from `std::cin` into the variable, so the arrows point at the variable: `std::cin >> variable;`. ? The person types `John Smith`. What does `std::cin >> name;` store? - `John Smith` - `Smith` + `John` - Nothing, because the input contains a space > Reading with `>>` stops at the first space, so `name` gets only `John`. `Smith` is left waiting for the next read. ? What is the difference between `std::cout << "age";` and `std::cout << age;`? - There is none; both print the value of `age` - The first prints the value; the second prints the word *age* + The first prints the word *age*; the second prints the value stored in `age` > Text in quotes is printed exactly as written. Without quotes, `age` is the name of a variable, so its value is printed. ? Why does `std::cout << "Hello" << "World";` print `HelloWorld`? - Each `<<` removes the spaces from the text - `std::cout` can only print one word at a time - The second `<<` overwrites the first word + `std::cout` adds no spaces of its own > `std::cout` prints exactly what you give it and adds nothing between items. Put the space inside the quotes: `"Hello "`. ```
ideas:
1. Ask for two numbers and print their sum.
2. Ask for a full name with `std::getline` and greet the person.
3. Print this small table using `\t` between the columns:
```
Item    Price
Apple   0.5
Bread   2.25
```

cards.q: Which way do the arrows point for input?
cards.a:
`std::cin >> variable;`, from the keyboard into the variable

For input the data moves from `std::cin` into the variable, so the arrows point at the variable: `std::cin >> variable;`.

cards.q: The person types `John Smith`. What does `std::cin >> name;` store?
cards.a:
`John`

Reading with `>>` stops at the first space, so `name` gets only `John`. `Smith` is left waiting for the next read.

cards.q: What is the difference between `std::cout << "age";` and `std::cout << age;`?
cards.a:
The first prints the word *age*; the second prints the value stored in `age`

Text in quotes is printed exactly as written. Without quotes, `age` is the name of a variable, so its value is printed.

`std::cout` adds no spaces of its own

`std::cout` prints exactly what you give it and adds nothing between items. Put the space inside the quotes: `"Hello "`.
